Part I: Introduction¶

  • Substantive

    • Title: Flavors of London- Mapping Restaurants and Cafés
    • Big idea and Message: This map helps users to explore London's vibrant food scene. Through this map, users can seamlessly navigate various categories, including coffee shops, sweet and dessert shops, wine bars, and a variety of other restaurants. this don't just highlight restaurants and cafes; but also provide a comprehensive guide that includes restaurant images, location, ratings, and links for detailed information.

  • Technical

    • Interactivity: Yes
    • Zoomable: Yes
    • Tooltips: Yes
    • Basemap: yes
    • Choropleth: yes
    • Technology: Python, Folium, Leaflet provider, RESTful Web APIs, Choropleth Mapping

  • Datasets

    • Shape File:

      • Source provider: Greater London Authority - "Greater London Authority"
      • File: London_Borough_Excluding_MHW.shp

    • Geo Jason Filee:

      • Source provider: Cartography Vectors - "Cartography Vectors"
      • File: london_421.geojson

    • Webservices-API:

      • Source provider: yelp - "yelp developer portal"
      • API URL: https://api.yelp.com/v3/businesses/search

  • Conceptualization and Implementation

    • My aim in creating this map is to provide users with a complete guide to exploring London's diverse food scene. Instead of just showing where restaurants are, this map helps users discover the wide range of dining options available in the city. With distinct markers and icons, users can easily find coffee shops, dessert spots, wine bars, and more, each offering its own unique culinary experience. Additionally, the map includes ratings and clickable links so users can learn more about each place before visiting. Oh, and there's also a tag in the tooltip indicating if a restaurant is cheap (£), mid-range (££), or fancy (£££).
    • In essence, this map goes beyond traditional mapping tools; it's like having a knowledgeable foodie friend right by your side, revealing the best dining spots London has to offer.

  • Data Sourcing and Integration

    • Part1: I set out to find an open-source API that could provide me with the necessary data for my map, including coordinates(lat and long), image URLs, addresses, and other pertinent information. After extensive research, I discovered the Yelp API, which offered free access to the data I required. Upon creating a free account with 'Yelp for Developers' and obtaining a client ID and API key through email verification, I explore the various endpoints provided by the yelp api. I carefully and precisely examined the request and response parameters of the 'https://api.yelp.com/v3/businesses/search' endpoint, understood the importance of each element. Utilizing Postman (software tool to test API), I tested the API and received a successful response with a 200 code, containing all the essential details such as image URLs, latitude, longitude, addresses, restaurant ratings, and price ranges. This something made my decision to utilize the Yelp API for restaurant data in my map.
    • Part2: to create static and choropleth maps, I required a shapefile delineating the boundaries of London. I scoured the internet and discovered an appropriate boundary shapefile of London from the Greater London Authority, which I promptly stored in my data folder.
    • Part3: to define the boundary of London and enable choropleth visualization in my interactive map, I downloaded a GeoJSON file from Cartography Vectors. Integrating this file into my map facilitated the visualization of London's boundaries and enhanced the overall user experience.map.

  • Code Description

    • The code provided utilizes the Yelp API, which allow us to access information about various businesses, here i am fetching data for coffee shops, dessert places, wine and beer establishments. The Yelp API provides access to a vast database of business data, including details such as business names, addresses, ratings, and categories. In this code, an API key provided by Yelp is used to authenticate requests to the Yelp API.
    • The search_yelp function sends requests to the Yelp API endpoint for business search (https://api.yelp.com/v3/businesses/search) with specific search terms like 'coffee', 'desserts', and 'beer_and_wine' for locations in London.
    • However, a limitation of the Yelp API is its restriction to returning only 50 datasets in a single request. To overcome this limitation, I implemented pagination by incrementing the offset value, allowing me to fetch additional data for my map.By making multiple requests with different offset values, the function fetches a wide range of data for each category
    • the code runs the search_yelp function 30 times, fetching 500 datasets for each category. Total 1500 data fetched in 58 seconds.The results are then combined into a single dataset named combined_results.
In [2]:
def search_yelp(search_term):
    API_KEY = 'x7TJrTMBO3BuU6lGhCYEyYg4s-b4wdfBRktbuec33CXe5-O5bnxCcSG3_rigxOThgjr4SszJwlCSr5RqNIo57gz377jSPAJFmtoz9NlsxXP0Z4mDDzB-xy83cvnhZXYx'
    LOCATION = 'london' # lodon is selected as my prefered location, we can change this location according to our required city or country
    url = 'https://api.yelp.com/v3/businesses/search' # this is the endpoint of yelp API
    headers = {'Authorization': f'Bearer {API_KEY}'} 
    limit = 50
    offset = 0 #Initialize the offset to fect different dataset pagination
    num_iterations = 10 # 10 times for one category serch API will be called
    all_results = []

    for _ in range(num_iterations):
        params = {'term': search_term, 'location': LOCATION, 'limit': limit, 'offset': offset}
        response = requests.get(url, headers=headers, params=params) #Send a GET request to the Yelp API with api key in header and all re request parameter
        data = response.json() # storing json response 
        businesses = data['businesses']
        all_results.extend(businesses)
        offset += limit

    return all_results

coffee_shops = search_yelp('coffee')
dessert_places = search_yelp('desserts')
beer_and_wine = search_yelp('beer_and_wine')

combined_results = coffee_shops + dessert_places + beer_and_wine

Part II: Static Mapping¶

  • Data Preparation:
    • The restaurant data from Yelp API is collected and stored in a DataFrame called 'resturants_df'
    • The latitude and longitude coordinates are extracted from the 'coordinates' column and stored in separate columns.
    • The 'alias' and 'title' columns are created to extract the category alias and title from the 'categories' column.
    • The DataFrame is converted into a GeoDataFrame 'gdf' to enable plotting geographic data.
In [4]:
resturants_df = pd.DataFrame(combined_results) #  converting jason response into panda DataFrame

resturants_df[['latitude', 'longitude']] = resturants_df['coordinates'].apply(lambda x: pd.Series([x['latitude'], x['longitude']]))
resturants_df[['alias', 'title']] = resturants_df['categories'].apply(lambda x: pd.Series([x[0]['alias'], x[0]['title']]))

# Convert DataFrame to GeoDataFrame to plot cordinates in static map
gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(resturants_df, geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(resturants_df.longitude, resturants_df.latitude))
  • Categorization:
    • A function 'map_alias' is defined to map restaurant aliases to broader categories such as 'coffee', 'sweets_n_desserts', 'wine_bars', and 'restaurants'
    • This function is applied to create a new column 'new_alias' in both the 'resturants_df' and 'gdf' DataFrames, categorizing the restaurants.
In [5]:
# Define a function to map aliases to new aliases
def map_alias(alias):
    if alias in ['coffee', 'cafes', 'coffeeroasteries','tea','cafeteria']:
        return 'coffee'
    elif alias in ['bakeries', 'icecream', 'cakeshop', 'donuts','chocolate','desserts','pancakes','waffles']:
        return 'sweets_n_desserts'
    elif alias in ['bars', 'wine_bars', 'whiskeybars']:
        return 'wine_bars'
    elif alias in ['breakfast_brunch', 'restaurants', 'diners']:
        return 'restaurants'
    else:
        return alias

# Apply the function to create the new column
resturants_df['new_alias'] = resturants_df['alias'].apply(map_alias)
# Apply the function to create the new column
gdf['new_alias'] = gdf['alias'].apply(map_alias) #adding this new alias in geo data frame to categories the plots

  • Plotting:
    • CRS of the GeoDataFrame 'gdf' is set to WGS84 (EPSG:4326) initially and data is projected to the British Grid - London (EPSG:27700) to match the boundary shapefile. taken from : https://epsg.io/?q=great+britain
    • This function is applied to create a new column 'new_alias' in both the 'resturants_df' and 'gdf' DataFrames, categorizing the restaurants.
    • Colors and marker styles are defined for each restaurant category
    • Restaurants are plotted on the map using different colors and marker styles based on their categories.
    • The boundary layer is plotted with black edges to outline the boroughs.
    • A basemap from CartoDB.Positron is added to the map with contextily. taken from : https://xyzservices.readthedocs.io/en/stable/introduction.html
In [6]:
# Setting the Coordinate Reference System (CRS) to WGS84 (EPSG:4326)
gdf.set_crs(epsg=4326, inplace=True)
# project to British Grid -London
gdf.to_crs(epsg= 27700, inplace = True)
boundary_gdf = gpd.read_file('../data/ESRI/London_Borough_Excluding_MHW.shp')
boundary_gdf = boundary_gdf.to_crs(epsg=27700)  

# Define colors and marker styles for each category
category_styles = {
    'coffee': ('orange', 'o'),  # Circle marker for coffee
    'sweets_n_desserts': ('purple', '*'),  # Star marker for dessert
    'wine_bars': ('purple', 's'),  # Square marker for wine bars
    'restaurants': ('green', 'd')  # Diamond marker for restaurants
}

# Plotting restaurants on a map with different colors and marker styles based on category
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(8, 10))

# Iterate over each category and plot it with the corresponding color and marker style
for category, (color, marker) in category_styles.items():
    category_gdf = gdf[gdf['new_alias'] == category]
    category_gdf.plot(ax=ax, color=color, markersize=5, marker=marker, label=category)

# Plot the boundary layer
    boundary_gdf.plot(ax=ax, color='none', edgecolor='black', linewidth=0.1)

# Add basemap
ctx.add_basemap(ax, crs=boundary_gdf.crs, source=ctx.providers.CartoDB.Positron)

# Set title and legend
ax.set_title('Flavors of London')
ax.legend()

plt.show()

Part III: Choropleth Mapping¶

  • Data Merging:
    • Creating a choropleth map displaying restaurant ratings across London regions
    • The CRS of the 'restaurant_geo' GeoDataFrame is reprojected to match the CRS of the boundary shapefile of London regions ('boundary_gdf').
    • A spatial join is performed between the London regions (from 'boundary_gdf') and the restaurants (from 'restaurant_geo') based on their spatial relationship..
    • The join operation is based on containment, meaning each London region contains some restaurants within its boundaries
In [7]:
# Convert restaurant data to a GeoDataFrame and set CRS
restaurant_geo = gpd.GeoDataFrame(resturants_df, geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(resturants_df.longitude, resturants_df.latitude),crs='EPSG:4326')

# Reproject restaurant GeoDataFrame to match CRS of London regions
restaurant_geo = restaurant_geo.to_crs(boundary_gdf.crs)

# Perform spatial join based on nearest distance
merged_data = gpd.sjoin(boundary_gdf, restaurant_geo, how='left', op='contains')
  • Plotting Choropleth:
    • The merged data (London regions with restaurant ratings) is plotted as a choropleth map on the axis.
    • The color of each region is determined by its restaurant ratings, with a colormap ('Blues') applied.
    • A color scale (colorbar) is added to the plot to represent the range of restaurant ratings.
    • The colorbar is labeled with "Restaurant Ratings" and placed vertically next to the plot.
In [8]:
# Create a figure and axis
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(8, 6))

merged_data.plot(ax=ax, linewidth=0.3, cmap='Blues', legend=True) # Plot the merged data as a choropleth map
ax.set_axis_off()

# Set title
title_parameters = {'fontsize': '16', 'fontname': 'Times New Roman'}
ax.set_title("Flavors of London", **title_parameters)

# Add a color scale (colorbar)
# Create a colormap and normalize the colors
cmap = plt.cm.get_cmap('Blues')
norm = mcolors.Normalize(vmin=merged_data['rating'].min(), vmax=merged_data['rating'].max())

# Create the colorbar
sm = plt.cm.ScalarMappable(cmap=cmap, norm=norm)
sm.set_array([])  # Set an empty array since we don't need the colorbar to represent any specific values
cbar = plt.colorbar(sm, ax=ax, shrink=0.7)
cbar.set_label('Restaurant Ratings', rotation=90)  # Set the label for the colorbar

# Show the plot
plt.show()

Part IV: Interactive Mapping¶

  • Description:

    • This interactive map showcases the vibrant culinary landscape of London, overlaying restaurant locations on a detailed geographic map. The map is centered around London with a zoom level set to capture a comprehensive view. Utilizing GeoJSON data, London's administrative boundaries are outlined in blue, with a yellow fill to distinguish them from the surrounding area.

    • Markers are clustered together for improved readability, making it easy for users to explore numerous restaurant locations within close proximity. Each marker represents a unique dining establishment and provides essential information such as the restaurant name, rating, address, and price range. Additionally, a thumbnail image of the restaurant is displayed in the marker's popup, offering users a visual preview of the dining experience.

    • Users can interact with the map by clicking on individual markers to view detailed information about each restaurant. The popup window dynamically adjusts to accommodate the restaurant's name, rating, address, price range, and an optional image. Moreover, a tooltip displays the restaurant's name and rating upon hovering over the marker, allowing for quick insights into nearby dining options.

In [9]:

In [15]:
import folium
from folium import plugins

# Create map centered at the specified location
map_center = folium.Map(location=[51.51283552118349,-0.135955810546875], zoom_start=10) # selected london latitude and longitude and zoom level 10

# Add OpenStreetMap tile layer
folium.TileLayer('openstreetmap').add_to(map_center) 

# Add another tile layer (for example, Stamen Terrain) with attribution
folium.TileLayer('stamenterrain', attr='Stamen Terrain').add_to(map_center)

# Customize the appearance of the GeoJSON overlay
style_function = lambda x: {'color': 'blue', 'fillColor': 'yellow', 'weight': 2, 'opacity': 0.6}

# Add GeoJSON overlay to the map
folium.GeoJson(geojson_file, style_function=style_function).add_to(map_center)

# Create a marker cluster
marker_cluster = plugins.MarkerCluster().add_to(map_center)

# Add markers for each restaurant to the marker cluster
for business in combined_results:
    name = business['name']
    lat = business['coordinates']['latitude']
    lon = business['coordinates']['longitude']
    rating = business['rating']
    address = ', '.join(business['location']['display_address'])
    image_url = business.get('image_url')
    web_url = business.get('url')
    price = business.get('price')
    category = gdf['new_alias']  
    popup_text = f"<b>{name}</b><br>Rating: {rating}<br>Address: {address}<br>Price: {price}<br> <img src='{image_url}' width='200px'><br> <h5>Check out more <a href='{web_url}' target='_blank'>here</a></h5>"
    tooltip_text = f"{name} - Rating: {rating}"
    
    # Add marker to the marker cluster
    folium.Marker([lat, lon], popup=folium.Popup(popup_text, max_width=300), tooltip=tooltip_text).add_to(marker_cluster)
    
# Add layer control
folium.LayerControl().add_to(map_center)

# Display the map
map_center

Conclusion¶

  • "Flavors of London - Mapping Restaurants and Cafés" is a comprehensive guide that enables users to explore London's diverse culinary scene. Leveraging the Yelp API, the map provides detailed insights into various dining options, including coffee shops, dessert spots, and wine bars, empowering users to make informed choices. By efficiently fetching data and categorizing establishments, the map enhances user experience, simplifying navigation through London's bustling food landscape. Through the integration of static and choropleth mapping techniques, users can visualize restaurant distributions and ratings across the city's regions using interactive map. Ultimately, "Flavors of London" offers an immersive journey through the city's culinary delights, serving as a trusted companion for culinary exploration and discovery.
